title: Copper Plates Feed the Chandela Realm

title_i18n.en: Copper Plates Feed the Chandela Realm

subtitle: How grants, samantas, and merchants fed the temples of Jejakabhukti
region: Jejakabhukti, Kalinjar, Khajuraho and Gwalior feudatories
moral: Grand monuments stand on everyday institutions.

sources.citation: Satyabhama copper plate from Kundeshwar, 1004 CE; Nanyaura copper-plate grant of Dhanga, 998 CE
sources.note: Land-grant evidence for administration and Vidyadhara's revised chronology.

sources.citation: Dubkund inscription of Kachchhapaghata Arjuna; early Kalinjar Chandi Darwaza merchant inscription
sources.note: Evidence for samanta service and merchant communities.

sources.citation: B.D. Chattopadhyay, The Making of Early Medieval India (1994), pp. 183-220; Cynthia Talbot, Precolonial India in Practice (2001), ch. 3
sources.note: Modern frameworks for grants, political economy and inscriptional practice.

panels.shot: dramatic three-quarter view, low-angle, of Satyabhama holding up a gleaming copper plate against a backdrop of Khajuraho temples and distant forts

dialogue.text: Beneath the stone of Khajuraho, copper plates, village fields and samantas quietly fed the Chandela realm.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a copper plate being unearthed in a modern village field, time-blend hinting at past and present

dialogue.text: From Kundeshwar to Nanyaura, buried copper plates whisper how the Chandela kings ruled through land, water and promise.

panels.shot: medium shot of Satyabhama seated in a modest yet dignified household, with scribes nearby, scrolls and copper plates laid out

dialogue.text: Around 1004, Satyabhama’s grant at Kundeshwar fixed a Chandela king’s date, but it also fixed a village’s fate.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up of the copper plate surface as letters are incised, with a faint reflection of Satyabhama’s face

dialogue.text: The inscription names gifts of land and rights, a precise place, a purpose, a king, a donor, and the witnesses who will remember.

panels.shot: wide rural landscape shot showing a village, tanks, fields and a distant temple under construction

dialogue.text: The plates speak of land and villages, not cities alone: of fields, tanks, groves and the people bound to serve them.

panels.shot: medium shot of a samanta chieftain at the Dubkund region, presenting himself at court with folded hands

dialogue.text: In Dubkund, Arjuna of the Kachchhapaghatas left stone words that he served the Chandela king Vidyadhara as samanta, a feudatory yet a lord in his own land.

panels.shot: split-scene composition: left side showing Arjuna leading troops, right side showing him presiding over local justice and land

dialogue.text: As samanta, Arjuna owed military service and loyalty; in return he held land, collected dues and carved his own name into the stone of Dubkund.

panels.shot: medium temple-entrance shot of merchants at Kalinjar’s Chandi Darwaza, with their inscription panel in view

dialogue.text: At Kalinjar’s Chandi Darwaza, early merchant inscriptions record gifts, routes and names, tying distant traders to this hill of gods and kings.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of the Kalinjar gateway with caravans passing underneath, pilgrims and soldiers mingling

dialogue.text: The fort became a node: merchants sought protection and prestige, kings sought taxes and honour, temples sought steady offerings.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of a temple accountant counting coins and weighing grain in a Khajuraho shrine store-room

dialogue.text: Temple endowments were not stone alone; inscriptions describe fields, oil-presses, markets and shares of produce feeding the lamps and the priests.

panels.shot: wide shot of a water tank near Khajuraho with pilgrims and vendors around its steps

dialogue.text: Water, too, became wealth: tanks endowed by grants drew pilgrims, who in turn drew traders and craftsmen, weaving a small economy around each sacred shore.

panels.shot: close-up of Madanavarman-era coins being poured from a cloth bag into a merchant’s hand

dialogue.text: Under Madanavarman, coins appear in abundance, a late sign that the Chandela realm still pulsed with trade and payments when stone building slowed.

panels.shot: medium shot of Satyabhama handing the Kundeshwar copper plate to assembled brahmana donees and village elders

dialogue.text: Guard this grant, and the land will guard you.

panels.shot: close-up on the gathered faces of villagers reacting as the grant is proclaimed aloud by a scribe

dialogue.text: Such grants conferred tax exemptions and duties, shifting who paid whom and who could claim the sweat of these fields.

panels.shot: scholarly montage: modern historians comparing inscriptions, maps and coins on a table, with Chandela sites faint in the background

dialogue.text: Modern scholars, from B.D. Chattopadhyay to Cynthia Talbot, piece together this economy from scattered plates, stones and coins, not from a neat archive.

panels.shot: reflective wide shot at dusk of Khajuraho’s temples above darkening fields and a village, Satyabhama’s silhouette faint in the foreground

dialogue.text: The Chandela order was not a copy of distant feudal worlds, but its own web of samantas, grants and markets, where copper plates quietly held up towers of stone.
